newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel rejects Sequus' Amphotec.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel rejects Sequus' Amphotec.

text.p: A Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advisory panel on Monday rejected Sequus Pharmaceuticals Inc's Amphotec as a treatment for febrile neutropenia in patients who fail to respond to anti-bacterial therapy.

The panel voted 8-0 that Amphotec (amphotericin B cholesteryl sulfate complex), a liposomal formulation of amphotericin B, was safer than the older product, but voted 7-1 that Sequus had not shown efficacy. "We're a victim of insufficient data," said panel chairman Dr. Scott Hammer of the Harvard Medical School.
The FDA is not bound by the panel's advice but usually follows it.

A recommendation for approval would have meant that Amphotec would be the first antifungal that could be given to patients without specific documentation of fungal infection, giving it an edge over competitors.

About 1.5-to-2 million Americans experience febrile neutropenia, usually due to high-dose chemotherapy, AIDS, or organ transplantation. Menlo Park, Calif.-based Sequus estimates that close to half of these patients do not respond to antibacterial drugs, and would be eligible for Amphotec.
Also, the drug was engineered to decrease the toxic kidney effects seen with amphotericin B.

There are several other liposomal forms of amphotericin B on the market, including NeXstar Pharmaceuticals Inc's Ambisome and Liposome Co's Abelcet. None have been approved specifically for treatment of febrile neutropenia at the doctor's discretion.

Doctors say they reluctantly use them off-label, as therapy can cost $400 to $500 a day. They usually wait to see if antibacterials resolve the fever, or to get a definitive diagnosis of fungal infection before prescribing antifungals.
Sequus presented data from one randomized clinical trial that it said showed that Amphotec worked as well as amphotericin B, also known as Fungizone.

In the 213-patient study, Sequus showed that half the Amphotec patients had a "successful outcome" -- they lived at least a week past the study's completion, had their fever resolved, and had not dropped out due to toxicity -- compared to 43% of Fungizone patients.
Four percent in each group developed a fungal infection during the study.
Sequus vice president Dr. Marc Gurwith said Amphotec was safer than amphotericin B, noting that 20 percent of Amphotec patients had kidney toxicity compared to half the Fungizone group.

FDA medical reviewers agreed that Sequus had shown Amphotec was less toxic, but questioned the firm's conclusions about treatment effect, noting that the study was not orginally designed to prove efficacy. FDA statistician Dr. Liji Shen said that there is "still considerable uncertainty of comparability between Amphotec and Fungizone," so the drugs could not be considered equivalent.

David Feigal, director of the FDA's Office of Drug Evaluation IV, told the panel that "a product does not have to meet equivalence to be approved." But committee members said they wanted more conclusive data.

Amphotec was approved by the FDA in November 1996 for patients with invasive aspergillosis who don't respond to amphotericin B. It is approved in Europe as a second-line therapy for a number of opportunistic infections.
In fiscal 1996, Sequus reported a loss of $17.1 million on sales of $32.9 million. Trading in Sequus' stock was halted Monday morning in anticipation of the panel meeting.
